expectations.text: States Naidoo's nuanced position on gluten (sensitivity varies, not universal ban)
expectations.evidence: 'Gluten is clearly a problem for people with coeliac disease... non-coeliac gluten sensitivity... She does not say everyone should go gluten-free.' This matches the book's conditional position, though it is hedged 'as I recall the book'.

It is factually wrong against the book: 'MSG is not a major theme of her book' and 'MSG barely features in her advice.' In fact, MSG, glutamates and glutamic acid are on the PTSD (p.98) and OCD (p.157-158) avoid lists, with a long food list. It gives general research on MSG instead of her position.

expectations.text: Gives her caffeine guidance as a limit rather than a ban
expectations.evidence: It does say she 'doesn't require everyone to cut it out entirely', but it never gives her actual guidance (under 400 mg a day, none after 3 p.m.). Instead it offers a non-book target ('about 1-2 cups... before noon'). It also misstates her ADHD position ('mixed, modest effect. It isn't a treatment') when the ADHD cheat sheet says caffeine 'can help'.

expectations.text: Raises orthorexia as a risk of over-restriction
expectations.evidence: Section 4 defines orthorexia nervosa, lists warning signs, and says 'cutting three things at once... is a common way into this pattern.' It does not note that Naidoo herself covers orthorexia (Ch 7), but the assertion only requires raising the risk.

expectations.text: Recommends a measured approach (e.g. elimination trial, professional input)
expectations.evidence: Section 5 says to add before you subtract, change one thing at a time for 2-4 weeks and track it, test for coeliac disease before a structured gluten trial, and get help from a registered dietitian or therapist.
